title: How Peanut Butter Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about their favorite peanut butter brands and ways to eat it, then dig into the history of peanut butter. They cover peanuts as a legume originating in South America, their spread through Europe, Africa and back to the Americas via the slave trade, and their growth in the US from 1842 in Virginia. They discuss how peanuts were viewed as food for the poor, the Civil War, circus peanut galleries, Ben Hicks's peanut picker, and George Washington Carver. The main peanut butter history follows: Marcellus Gilmore Edson's 1884 Canadian patent, John Harvey Kellogg's nut butters, early fair debuts, WWI rations, hydrogenation, Peter Pan, Joseph Rosefield and Skippy, Jif, the FDA peanut butter standard and federal definition, USDA color standards, health and nutrition, aflatoxin and recall incidents, peanut allergy trends, and arachibutyrophobia. The episode ends with listener mail from Daniel.

segments.title: Banter about favorite peanut butter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke around and share how they like to eat peanut butter, including favorite brands, unusual combinations like mayonnaise and marshmallow fluff, and artisan natural varieties. They also chat about diet and quarantine eating.

segments.title: Peanuts origins and spread
segments.summary: The hosts explain that peanuts are a legume originating in South America, with evidence in Peruvian culture. Peanuts spread through Spanish and Portuguese explorers to Europe, Asia, Africa, and back to the Americas via the West African slave trade. Commercial US farming began in Virginia in 1842.

segments.title: Peanuts as food for the poor and early American uses
segments.summary: Peanuts were long considered food for the poor and livestock, and were used for oil and lubricant. The Civil War, P. T. Barnum's circus peanuts and the peanut gallery phrase, and the rise of street vendor peanuts are discussed. Hicks's peanut picker and George Washington Carver's work on peanuts after cotton depletion and the boll weevil are covered.

segments.title: Early peanut butter inventors
segments.summary: Marcellus Gilmore Edson Wallace, a Canadian, patented a paste of peanuts with sugar, described as having a consistency like butter, lard, or ointment. Dr. John Harvey Kellogg is described as an early peanut butter pioneer at Battle Creek. Debate about the first public debut at the 1904 St. Louis or Chicago World's Fair is covered.
topics: Marcellus Gilmore Edson Wallace peanut butter patent

segments.title: Peanut butter spreads, wars, and hydrogenation
segments.summary: Peanut butter sales grew rapidly by 1907, with companies like Hinz and Beech-Nut. It became part of military rations in the world wars. Hydrogenation, described in John Crampner's book, made peanut butter creamier and shelf stable but turned healthy fats saturated. Hydrogenated brands later outsold natural ones.

segments.title: Peter Pan, Skippy, and Jif brands
segments.summary: Peter Pan was the biggest early brand using a partial hydrogenation process patented by Joseph Rosefield. After a licensing dispute, Rosefield created Skippy, which became a top seller. Procter and Gamble owned Jif until 2001 or 2002, when it went to Smucker's. Jif remains a leading brand, and the name was chosen for being easy to spell, say, and remember.

segments.title: FDA standards, USDA grades, and peanut butter definition
segments.summary: The FDA in the 1960s pushed back on sugar and molasses additives, leading to a standard requiring peanuts, enforced in 1972. The federal definition sets smooth, medium, and crunchy textures. USDA color standards come from Aggtron, Inc. of Sparks, Nevada. Peanut butter accounts for about half of US edible peanut use, and about 540 peanuts go into a 12-ounce jar.

segments.title: Peanut butter health, contamination, and allergies
segments.summary: Recent peanut butter recalls in 2007 (Sam and Ella, Peter Pan, Great Value under ConAgra) and 2009 (Blakely, Georgia plant, with deaths) are discussed. Aflatoxins produced by Aspergillus mold are a concern. Nutrition facts and the benefits of natural peanut butter are covered. Peanut allergy rates in self-reports versus diagnoses, oral immunotherapy, and arachibutyrophobia (fear of peanut butter on the roof of the mouth) are discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail from Daniel
segments.summary: A listener named Daniel shares that he has listened since middle school, earned the nickname random fact kid, and got through electrical engineering with help from the show. He also mentions his friend Lucas, who listens while driving a bus.
